practice.thesis: I turn hard-to-see civic systems into instruments people can inspect, question, and improve.

works.title: The water beneath the dashboard
works.summary: A public observability system that joins maintenance records, sensor drift, and resident reports without flattening uncertainty.

caseStudy.challenge:
The city's water dashboard showed one confident number per district. Engineers, residents, and the council each knew it
was wrong in different ways, and none of them could say how.
caseStudy.context:
Twelve districts, three maintenance contractors, a sensor network with known drift, and a resident reporting line that
nobody had joined to the rest.
caseStudy.role: I led the research and the design of the evidence model, with two engineers from the water board.
caseStudy.constraints: No new sensors, no new staff, and every figure had to say where it came from, so a resident could check it.

decisions.decision: Show each figure with its sources and how far they disagree.
decisions.rationale: Disagreement was the information people needed, so hiding it made the dashboard less useful, not more.
decisions.alternatives: A single blended figure with a confidence badge, which the engineers had already stopped trusting.

decisions.decision: Put resident reports beside sensor readings, not under them.
decisions.rationale: Residents noticed failures days before the sensors drifted far enough to flag them.

caseStudy.evidence: Thirty-one interviews across the districts, and six months of reports matched against maintenance records.
caseStudy.outcomes:
Twelve districts now share one evidence model, and the council's quarterly review starts from the disagreements instead of
arguing about which number is right.
caseStudy.reflection:
The hardest part was persuading people that showing uncertainty was a feature. Next time I would bring residents into the
first workshop, not the third.
